title: The K-12 Hiring Timeline: When to Lock In Fall Special Education Staff
metaTitle: K-12 Hiring Timeline: When to Lock In Fall SPED Staff
description: A month-by-month K-12 hiring timeline, February to September: when to make offers, when resignations land and how to cover special education seats by day 1.

bodyHtml:
When should a district lock in fall special education and related-services staff?

In spring. Have offers out by May 1, and by mid-June have a coverage request on file for every seat that is still open. The candidates you want are choosing between districts in March, April and May, and your own vacancy list keeps moving until late July.

The May 1 date comes from TNTP's study of 4 urban districts that waited until July or August to make offers. Between 31% and almost 60% of their applicants withdrew, and 50% to 70% of those who left named the late timeline as a major reason. TNTP's recommendation: hire and place the vast majority of new teachers by May 1 each year (source: TNTP, Missed Opportunities, 2003). The Learning Policy Institute's advice to districts points to the same season: hire as early as possible, ideally in the spring of the prior school year (source: Learning Policy Institute, What Districts Can Do, 2016).

Before the 2024-25 school year began, public schools had filled 79% of their teaching vacancies with fully certified teachers, and 77% of their special education vacancies (source: NCES School Pulse Panel, October 17, 2024 release). In October 2024, 35% of public schools still had at least 1 teaching vacancy, and special education positions averaged 5% vacant (source: NCES School Pulse Panel, December 12, 2024 release). The federal rule sets its own date: "At the beginning of each school year, each public agency must have in effect, for each child with a disability within its jurisdiction, an IEP" (source: eCFR, 34 CFR 300.323(a)).

What does a school district recruitment calendar look like, February through September?

The calendar runs 8 months, and each month has a job that cannot be done later. Lines marked "practice" are operating steps. Every other line names its source, linked in the sections around the table. The printable planning calendar on this page turns it into a checklist.

Why is spring the turning point for SLPs, OTs and school psychologists?

Clinicians commit in spring, and their training runs on a full-year clock. A new SLP needs a 36-week clinical fellowship under a certified mentor, and a school psychology intern is placed for one academic year, so both are spoken for before summer.

New graduates are on a fixed clock

A new SLP cannot start a clinical fellowship until all graduate coursework and clinical practicum are complete. The fellowship then takes at least 36 weeks and 1,260 hours. The mentor must hold ASHA certification with at least 9 months of full-time experience after earning it, and owes at least 6 hours of direct and 6 hours of indirect supervision in each of the fellowship's 3 segments (source: ASHA, clinical fellowship requirements). Hiring a new graduate means naming a mentor at the same time.

For school psychologists, the NASP standard is a supervised internship of at least 1,200 clock hours, at least 600 of them in a school setting, completed across one academic year full time (source: National Association of School Psychologists, 2020 Professional Standards). The placement covers the whole year, so it is arranged before the year begins.

Supply is short before you post

  • Speech-language pathology. In ASHA's 2024 Schools Survey, 79% of school-based SLPs said there were more job openings than job seekers (source: ASHA, 2024 Schools Survey).
  • School psychology. NASP recommends 1 school psychologist for every 500 students. Its current national estimate is 1 for every 1,127 (source: National Association of School Psychologists, shortage of school psychologists).
  • Therapy disciplines. The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects about 12,500 openings a year for SLPs and about 10,000 for OTs from 2025 to 2035 (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, speech-language pathologists and occupational therapists).

FocusedEDU recruits all of these disciplines: see related services staffing.

Your own vacancy list is still moving

State law sets when a resignation or a non-renewal is final, and the dates run from May into late July. In TNTP's study, 3 of the 4 districts had a summer notification deadline for departing teachers or none at all.

StateWhat the law setsThe dateWhere it is written
PennsylvaniaA tenured professional ends the standard contract by written resignationPresented 60 days before it takes effectPublic School Code of 1949, Section 1121
New JerseyEach nontenured teaching staff member gets a written contract offer or a written notice that none will be offered. Paraprofessionals in Title I districts get the same noticeOn or before May 15N.J.S.A. 18A:27-10, quoted in Commissioner decision 194-21 and P.L. 2009, c. 227
DelawareA board that will not keep a teacher gives written notice of its intentionOn or before May 15Delaware Code, Title 14, § 1410
OhioNo teacher may terminate a contract after this date without the board's consentJuly 10Ohio Revised Code 3319.15
IllinoisA resignation submitted after the school year ends must reach the board secretary in writingAt least 30 calendar days before the first student attendance dayIllinois School Code, 105 ILCS 5/24-14

A planning example: your first student day is Tuesday, August 24, 2027. In Illinois, a resignation is on time through July 25. In Pennsylvania, a resignation presented on June 25 takes effect on the first day of school. A new SLP who starts on August 24 reaches the 36-week minimum on May 2, 2028 at the earliest. One who starts on November 1 reaches it on July 10, 2028, after a school year that closes in June.

By summer, the strongest candidates have signed elsewhere. In one district TNTP studied, the applicants who withdrew were 40% more likely than the people eventually hired to hold a degree in their teaching field, and 37% to 69% of the known withdrawers were candidates for hard-to-fill positions (source: TNTP, Missed Opportunities, 2003).

What does late hiring cost students and budgets?

It costs students measurable learning, and it costs the budget a second search. Papay and Kraft found that hiring teachers after the school year starts reduces student achievement by 0.042 standard deviations in math and 0.026 in reading (source: Papay and Kraft, Journal of Policy Analysis and Management, 2016 abstract). The Learning Policy Institute describes that study, of 130,000 students and 9,000 teachers in a large urban district, as a loss of about 2 months of instruction for a typical middle school student (source: Learning Policy Institute, Solving the Teacher Shortage, 2016).

Part of the loss is a first-year disruption. Part is who is left to hire: in math, late-hired teachers stayed less effective. The same review reports that late hires are more likely to leave teaching than other new hires.

  • The budget pays twice. Replacing 1 teacher costs $11,860 in a district under 10,000 students, $16,450 in a district of 10,000 to 50,000 and $24,930 in a district over 50,000 (source: Learning Policy Institute, 2024 technical supplement). A late hire who leaves in June brings that bill back. Price your own seat with the calculator in what an unfilled classroom costs a school district.
  • IEP services do not wait for the hire. Every IEP must be in effect when the school year begins, and for a new IEP, services must be made available "as soon as possible following development of the IEP" (source: eCFR, 34 CFR 300.323(a) and (c)(2)). When a state finds a failure to provide them, the corrective action is "such as compensatory services or monetary reimbursement" (source: eCFR, 34 CFR 300.151(b)(1)). Our guide to managing IEP backlogs and compensatory services covers the triage.
  • Evaluations keep their deadline. An initial evaluation must be conducted within 60 days of receiving parental consent, or within the state's own timeframe (source: eCFR, 34 CFR 300.301(c)(1)). An open school psychologist seat does not stop that count.

Early hiring pays the other way. When Boston Public Schools opened hiring earlier and ended forced placements, its median hire date moved up by more than 2 months, and the experience, effectiveness and retention of its new hires rose (source: Kraft, Papay, Wedenoja and Jones, 2021 paper).

Ask early and pay only for hours worked. The first step with FocusedEDU is a free 30-minute discovery call: no cost, no obligation. Contract staffing is paid by the hour worked, so a request for a seat you later fill yourself has no hours on it.

  1. The call. We map your open roles: disciplines, hours, buildings, and the certification or licensure each requires.
  2. The search. We source and interview candidates, verify the license and certification for the role, and complete clearances and reference checks.
  3. The shortlist. Your team interviews a short list of fully credentialed candidates and makes the final call.
  4. The hire. Every placement is temp-to-perm at no cost. Evaluate the professional on the job, then hire permanently with no conversion fee and no buyout.

The pipeline is yours alone. FocusedEDU works with one partner per market, so the educators recruited for you are never shared with a competing school or district in your area. A request in April gives that pipeline 4 months before the first student day. A request in August gives it days.

What should a district do in August when school starts with open seats?

Cover every IEP caseload with a qualified professional on day 1, then keep recruiting behind that coverage. The duty to deliver services starts with the school year, whether or not the hire is finished.

  1. Count open seats by caseload. For each seat, list the students, the IEP minutes owed each week and the evaluations due.
  2. Put certified and licensed professionals on special education first. Federal rule bars certification or licensure "waived on an emergency, temporary, or provisional basis" for special education teachers and related services personnel (source: eCFR, 34 CFR 300.156). A certified contract teacher or licensed clinician meets that bar. See special education staffing.
  3. Use substitutes where they fit. A substitute holds a general education classroom while the search continues. See substitute teacher staffing.
  4. Log minutes from the first day. Track delivered and missed IEP minutes by student, so the IEP team works from a record.
  5. Hand every late starter the caseload. Each provider must have access to the IEPs they implement and be told their specific responsibilities (source: eCFR, 34 CFR 300.323(d)). Have the schedule and caseload list ready on the first morning.
  6. Keep the search open, then convert. A contract professional who fits can become your permanent hire. The steps are in how to fill K-12 teacher vacancies quickly.

At First Philadelphia Public Charter School, 100% of open special education teacher roles were filled, each one within 2 weeks of the request, with 100% retention of the educators placed.

faqs.q: When is teacher hiring season for K-12 districts?
faqs.a: Spring. In one district TNTP studied, applications peaked in March. Neighboring districts finished most hiring by early summer, and 3 neighbors of one district had hired most of their new teachers by the end of May. TNTP recommends hiring and placing the vast majority of new teachers by May 1. The Learning Policy Institute advises districts to run hiring as early as possible, ideally in the spring of the prior school year.

faqs.q: When should a district hire special education teachers for fall?
faqs.a: Make offers by May 1 and request contract coverage by mid-June for any seat still open. Special education is hard to fill late: before the 2024-25 school year began, public schools had filled 77% of special education vacancies with fully certified teachers, according to NCES. Federal rule requires an IEP to be in effect for each child at the beginning of the school year.

faqs.q: What are the effects of late teacher hiring on students?
faqs.a: Papay and Kraft (2016) found that hiring teachers after the school year starts reduces student achievement by 0.042 standard deviations in math and 0.026 in reading. The Learning Policy Institute describes that as about 2 months of instruction for a typical middle school student. Part of the loss is a first-year disruption. In math, late-hired teachers stayed less effective.

faqs.q: How much notice does a teacher have to give before resigning?
faqs.a: It depends on the state. Pennsylvania's standard contract ends by a written resignation presented 60 days before it takes effect. Ohio bars a teacher from terminating a contract after July 10 without the board's consent. Illinois requires a summer resignation in writing at least 30 calendar days before the first student attendance day. Your collective bargaining agreement may add its own dates.

faqs.q: When are new speech-language pathologists and school psychologists available to hire?
faqs.a: A new SLP can start a clinical fellowship only after finishing all coursework and practicum, and the fellowship runs at least 36 weeks and 1,260 hours under a certified mentor, per ASHA. School psychology interns complete at least 1,200 hours across one academic year, per NASP. Both are placed for a full school year, so districts arrange them in spring.

faqs.q: How many teaching positions are still vacant when school starts?
faqs.a: Before the 2024-25 school year began, public schools reported an average of 6 teaching vacancies and had filled 79% of them with fully certified teachers, according to NCES. For special education the figure was 77%. In October 2024, 35% of public schools still had at least 1 teaching vacancy, and 20% had more than 1.
